why: I read the statement as Pillai's uniform conjecture, where exponents are unknown too, because under the fixed-exponent reading it would be Siegel's classical theorem and not on an unsolved list. Read that way, the classical results each settle a restriction and count as case: fixed bases (Pólya, Bennett), fixed exponents (Siegel), and C = 1 (Tijdeman, Mihăilescu). All of them are digested and all predate the snapshot. None settles the whole statement, so none tiers as resolved. Styer 2024 was the close call. For bases up to 3600 it proves at most one exponent pair. But finiteness for any fixed bases was already known classically, so what it adds is a sharper count for a restriction that was already settled. That is a stronger form of a known case, not new movement on the finiteness statement, so I answered variant. The polynomial, Lucas, Fibonacci, convergent-denominator, prime-power and sum-form papers ask changed questions, so they are variants. No AI was involved in any event.
doubts: If Styer 2024 were scored case rather than variant, the problem would come out partial after the snapshot. I judged it variant because fixed-base finiteness is classical. The statement's quantifiers are ambiguous: A, B, C nonzero is not stated, and it does not say whether exponents are fixed. Under the fixed-exponent reading, Siegel 1929 would arguably settle the whole statement, which would make the problem open_stale. The classical events rest on a survey read through a summarising fetch, and Bennett rests on snippets only.
